hits.heading: ### S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
hits.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

hits.heading: ### R1 — Own idea: an integral test of the exterior model
hits.text: Take the ordinary exterior algebra of the free rank-four module with basis \(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2\), and put \(\xi=e_1\wedge f_1+e_2\wedge f_2\); then \(\xi^2=2e_1\wedge f_1\wedge e_2\wedge f_2\), so multiplication by \(\xi^2\) is multiplication by 2 from \(\Lambda^0\) to \(\Lambda^4\), not an integral isomorphism. More generally, the standard rank-\(2n\) symplectic bivector satisfies \(\xi^n=n!\,\mathrm{vol}\), giving the same obstruction for \(n\ge2\). Thus, under the ordinary meaning of the explicitly written exterior algebra and multiplication operator, the integral model does not satisfy the displayed hard-Lefschetz isomorphism in degree 0; rational coefficients, divided powers, or a different lattice would have to be specified in a reconstructed statement. None of those possible repairs is inserted into the transcription.

hits.heading: ### S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
hits.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

hits.heading: ### S17 — Finite-field Künneth projectors illustrate a narrower later result
hits.text: For smooth projective varieties over finite fields, Katz and Messing (1974, Theorem 2) construct rational algebraic Künneth projectors as rational combinations of graphs of Frobenius iterates, compatibly with the cohomology theories in their hypotheses. Their theorem also gives integral, theory-independent characteristic polynomials for integral degree-zero correspondences. These results strengthen two particular ingredients appearing in the letters, but the projector statement is published condition \(C\), not the draft's stronger inverse-operator condition \(C_\ell\). Moreover, rationality in the Cayley–Hamilton criterion still has to be coupled with the required algebraic complementary-degree isomorphisms.

hits.heading: ### R1 — Own idea: an integral test of the exterior model
hits.text: Take the ordinary exterior algebra of the free rank-four module with basis \(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2\), and put \(\xi=e_1\wedge f_1+e_2\wedge f_2\); then \(\xi^2=2e_1\wedge f_1\wedge e_2\wedge f_2\), so multiplication by \(\xi^2\) is multiplication by 2 from \(\Lambda^0\) to \(\Lambda^4\), not an integral isomorphism. hits.text: Over \(k=\mathbb F_2\), the finite étale algebra \(R=k^3\) has no single algebra generator: every element has only two possible coordinate values, and its polynomial functions cannot separate all three factors. Neither requirement mentions the chosen ample class, so—once the criterion's hypotheses hold for the fixed theory—the argument applies to another polarization through its own hard Lefschetz isomorphism. Kleiman (1968, §§2.9–2.10) proves this criterion and polarization independence. This reasoning does not itself produce one cycle working for every \(\ell\), identify the draft's undefined \(D_\ell\), or justify removing every parameter in scan 44.

hits.heading: ### S16 — A nilpotent kernel is not a zero kernel
hits.text: Under algebraicity of the Künneth components, Jannsen (1992, Corollary 1) identifies the kernel from homological to numerical degree-zero correspondence algebras with the Jacobson radical and proves it nilpotent. This isolates a precise obstruction to obtaining the draft's cohomological semisimplicity from numerical semisimplicity. Nilpotence alone permits a nonzero ideal, so it is not a proof that the two equivalence relations coincide; an additional positivity or equivalence argument must annihilate that kernel. The distinction also prevents treating a numerical projector as a canonical cohomological projector solely because some lift exists.

hits.heading: ### S17 — Finite-field Künneth projectors illustrate a narrower later result
hits.text: For smooth projective varieties over finite fields, Katz and Messing (1974, Theorem 2) construct rational algebraic Künneth projectors as rational combinations of graphs of Frobenius iterates, compatibly with the cohomology theories in their hypotheses. Their theorem also gives integral, theory-independent characteristic polynomials for integral degree-zero correspondences. These results strengthen two particular ingredients appearing in the letters, but the projector statement is published condition \(C\), not the draft's stronger inverse-operator condition \(C_\ell\). Moreover, rationality in the Cayley–Hamilton criterion still has to be coupled with the required algebraic complementary-degree isomorphisms.

hits.heading: ### S19 — The Hodge reference is identifiable; the reception claim is not verified
hits.text: The publisher identifies Hodge's (1938) article as *Algebraic correspondences between surfaces*, pages 226–242, with DOI 10.1112/plms/s2-44.3.226, matching the letter's title, volume, opening page, and year. The accessible publisher record establishes that bibliographic identification, but the article's full text was not obtained in this research pass, so no additional theorem is attributed to it here. The letter reports Tate as intermediary for the projector attribution and adds a judgment about nearly thirty years of neglect; verifying that reception history would require evidence beyond identifying the cited paper.

hits.heading: ### S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
hits.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

hits.heading: ### S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
hits.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

hits.heading: ### R1 — Own idea: an integral test of the exterior model
hits.text: Take the ordinary exterior algebra of the free rank-four module with basis \(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2\), and put \(\xi=e_1\wedge f_1+e_2\wedge f_2\); then \(\xi^2=2e_1\wedge f_1\wedge e_2\wedge f_2\), so multiplication by \(\xi^2\) is multiplication by 2 from \(\Lambda^0\) to \(\Lambda^4\), not an integral isomorphism. More generally, the standard rank-\(2n\) symplectic bivector satisfies \(\xi^n=n!\,\mathrm{vol}\), giving the same obstruction for \(n\ge2\). Thus, under the ordinary meaning of the explicitly written exterior algebra and multiplication operator, the integral model does not satisfy the displayed hard-Lefschetz isomorphism in degree 0; rational coefficients, divided powers, or a different lattice would have to be specified in a reconstructed statement. None of those possible repairs is inserted into the transcription.

hits.heading: ### R6 — Own idea: a finite-field obstruction to the polynomial argument
hits.text: Over \(k=\mathbb F_2\), the finite étale algebra \(R=k^3\) has no single algebra generator: every element has only two possible coordinate values, and its polynomial functions cannot separate all three factors. Nevertheless, after extending scalars to an algebraic closure there are elements with three distinct coordinates, so the Vandermonde discriminant polynomial is not the zero polynomial. Thus passage to the algebraic closure proves polynomial nonvanishing without proving existence of a \(k\)-rational point of its nonvanishing locus. This is a conditional objection to the argument as preserved on this sheet, because an infinitude hypothesis may have been supplied in the antecedent text that is not present here.

hits.heading: ### R22 — Own idea: test the finite-fibre criterion without hidden flatness
hits.text: If this is read without further ambient hypotheses, let \(A=k[t]\) and \(B=A\times A/(t)\), with the diagonal \(A\)-algebra structure; then \(B\) is finite and its fibre at every maximal ideal is either \(k(\mathfrak m)\) or \(k(\mathfrak m)\times k(\mathfrak m)\), hence is finite étale. But \(B\simeq A\oplus A/(t)\) as an \(A\)-module is not flat, since multiplication by \(t\) kills a nonzero element, so \(B/A\) is not étale. Accordingly, the proposed equivalence needs the hypotheses of the referenced text to supply flatness or a condition that forces it; the counterexample does not decide whether those hypotheses were already in force. Using a product with the \(A\)-factor ensures that every fibre is nonempty, so this objection is not an artefact of allowing the zero algebra as an empty cover.

The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

hits.heading: ### R17 — Unpursued implication: the proposed nilpotent appendix is a categorical statement
hits.text: Finite étale covers are indeed invariant under nilpotent thickenings, and the modern statement allows arbitrary thickenings of schemes (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BQB, Lemma 58.8.3). For the proposed appendix, one must prove both lifting of finite étale algebras and unique lifting of their morphisms; existence of lifted defining equations alone proves neither the full equivalence nor its functoriality. The statement concerns the category of covers, and is compatible with the underlying scheme retaining its nilpotent structure.

hits.heading: ### S7 — Hard Lefschetz supplies linear inverses, not their cycles
hits.text: Deligne (1980, Theorem 4.1.1) proves hard Lefschetz for an ample class on a smooth projective variety over an algebraically closed field, with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients and \(\ell\) different from the characteristic: \(L^{n-i}:H^i\to H^{2n-i}\) is an isomorphism. Applied to the draft, this settles the existence of the indicated cohomological inverses in that setting, while the additional demand that an inverse arise from a rational algebraic correspondence remains a separate assertion. Keeping these two steps explicit also prevents the later theorem from concealing the integral obstruction in scan 14, where the coefficient ring is \(\mathbb Z\).

hits.heading: ### S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
hits.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

hits.heading: ### S15 — Numerical motives have a later unconditional theorem
hits.text: Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

hits.heading: ### S16 — A nilpotent kernel is not a zero kernel
hits.text: Under algebraicity of the Künneth components, Jannsen (1992, Corollary 1) identifies the kernel from homological to numerical degree-zero correspondence algebras with the Jacobson radical and proves it nilpotent. This isolates a precise obstruction to obtaining the draft's cohomological semisimplicity from numerical semisimplicity. Nilpotence alone permits a nonzero ideal, so it is not a proof that the two equivalence relations coincide; an additional positivity or equivalence argument must annihilate that kernel. The distinction also prevents treating a numerical projector as a canonical cohomological projector solely because some lift exists.

hits.heading: ### S17 — Finite-field Künneth projectors illustrate a narrower later result
hits.text: For smooth projective varieties over finite fields, Katz and Messing (1974, Theorem 2) construct rational algebraic Künneth projectors as rational combinations of graphs of Frobenius iterates, compatibly with the cohomology theories in their hypotheses. Their theorem also gives integral, theory-independent characteristic polynomials for integral degree-zero correspondences. These results strengthen two particular ingredients appearing in the letters, but the projector statement is published condition \(C\), not the draft's stronger inverse-operator condition \(C_\ell\). Moreover, rationality in the Cayley–Hamilton criterion still has to be coupled with the required algebraic complementary-degree isomorphisms.

hits.text: Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

hits.heading: ### S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
hits.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

hits.heading: ### R1 — Own idea: an integral test of the exterior model
hits.text: Take the ordinary exterior algebra of the free rank-four module with basis \(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2\), and put \(\xi=e_1\wedge f_1+e_2\wedge f_2\); then \(\xi^2=2e_1\wedge f_1\wedge e_2\wedge f_2\), so multiplication by \(\xi^2\) is multiplication by 2 from \(\Lambda^0\) to \(\Lambda^4\), not an integral isomorphism. More generally, the standard rank-\(2n\) symplectic bivector satisfies \(\xi^n=n!\,\mathrm{vol}\), giving the same obstruction for \(n\ge2\). Thus, under the ordinary meaning of the explicitly written exterior algebra and multiplication operator, the integral model does not satisfy the displayed hard-Lefschetz isomorphism in degree 0; rational coefficients, divided powers, or a different lattice would have to be specified in a reconstructed statement. None of those possible repairs is inserted into the transcription.

hits.heading: ### R6 — Own idea: a finite-field obstruction to the polynomial argument
hits.text: Over \(k=\mathbb F_2\), the finite étale algebra \(R=k^3\) has no single algebra generator: every element has only two possible coordinate values, and its polynomial functions cannot separate all three factors. Nevertheless, after extending scalars to an algebraic closure there are elements with three distinct coordinates, so the Vandermonde discriminant polynomial is not the zero polynomial. Thus passage to the algebraic closure proves polynomial nonvanishing without proving existence of a \(k\)-rational point of its nonvanishing locus. This is a conditional objection to the argument as preserved on this sheet, because an infinitude hypothesis may have been supplied in the antecedent text that is not present here.

hits.text: Over \(k=\mathbb F_2\), the finite étale algebra \(R=k^3\) has no single algebra generator: every element has only two possible coordinate values, and its polynomial functions cannot separate all three factors. Thus passage to the algebraic closure proves polynomial nonvanishing without proving existence of a \(k\)-rational point of its nonvanishing locus. hits.heading: ### S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
hits.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.
